content: Calcium citrate is the calcium salt derived from citric acid. It is frequently utilized as a food additive, designated as E333, primarily serving as a preservative, though it is occasionally employed to enhance flavor. In this regard, it shares similarities with sodium citrate. Additionally, calcium citrate functions as a water softener due to the ability of citrate ions to chelate undesirable metal ions. It is also a component in certain dietary calcium supplements. Chemically, calcium citrate possesses a sour taste, akin to citric acid. However, like other salts, it also exhibits a salty flavor. This combination of sour and salty characteristics has led to citrate compounds, such as sodium citrate and calcium citrate, being commonly referred to as sour salts. In industrial production, calcium citrate serves as an intermediate in the extraction of citric acid during the fermentation process. The citric acid present in the broth solution is neutralized using calcium hydroxide, resulting in the precipitation of insoluble calcium citrate. This precipitate is subsequently filtered out from the broth and thoroughly washed to yield purified calcium citrate. The resulting calcium citrate can either be marketed in its current form or converted back into citric acid through the application of dilute sulfuric acid. From a biological perspective, calcium citrate supplements have been associated with an increased risk of aluminum toxicity. This risk is particularly pronounced in patients with renal disease, where the toxicity potential is approximately five times higher compared to calcium carbonate. Consequently, individuals who have undergone Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery, a common form of weight-loss surgery, are typically advised to use calcium citrate as their preferred dietary calcium supplement.
